path: Idea-level briefs across dither, effects, shaders, data, and immersive. No reference component's code or page is read: every component follows the published methods named in its credits, and those sources were resolved before this file was written. Nothing fetches from the network, nothing adds a dependency, every random number comes from the seed, and every default already looks finished on the dark ground and the light one.

components.title: Dither Temporal
components.brief: A still subject whose two-tone screen renews itself every frame while its tone holds. The subject is the built-in lit sphere from lib/subject.ts, or a plain linear gradient, reduced to ink and ground on a canvas at a chosen pixel scale with unsmoothed pixels. It is for a background or a picture that has a faint living grain, like a print being screened again and again rather than a picture that moves. At a glance nothing translates, nothing grows, and no shape changes: only which dots carry the grey. It follows Ulichney's void-and-cluster method, whose mask lib/dither-mask.ts supplies, and takes from Wolfe and colleagues the requirement that successive masks stay blue over time as well as over space, so a second of frames averages to an even grey instead of a mottled one; the per-frame shift comes from the same module. The default frame at 1200 ms shows the sphere fully formed and lit from the upper left, its terminator carried by an even fine stipple, with no clumps, no tile seam, and no change in overall lightness. It is wrong if it reads as television static or if the picture appears to breathe: the tone at every point must measure the same at 1200 ms as at 3000 ms, and only the dot positions differ. It runs at 8 frames per second, and under reduced motion it holds one mask. Declare the facets animated, background, canvas, and dither, and let meta.palette list fg. Dither components have 6144 bytes and this one is expected near 4.3 KB. It fetches nothing, adds no dependency, takes every random number from the seed, and looks finished and intentional on both grounds.

components.title: Dither Reveal
components.brief: A photograph that arrives one dot at a time. Pixels turn on in the order a blue-noise mask gives, so at every moment the frame is an even halftone of the whole picture that thickens, never a wipe, a fade, or a half-drawn picture. It dissolves in over `reveal` ms, holds for `hold` ms, dissolves out again, and repeats, as a pure function of time. It is for an image that introduces itself at the top of a section. It follows Ulichney's void-and-cluster method for the order the dots arrive in, since each threshold of that mask adds the dots that fill the largest remaining gaps, which is exactly what an even reveal needs; the ordered dithering entry stands in for Bayer's matrix as the second mask, which reveals in a visible crosshatch instead. The picture is prepared once when the image loads and when the host resizes, into a copy no wider than 480 px, as registry/effects/pixel-sort already does; every frame afterwards only draws from that prepared copy, and nothing reads pixels back per frame. Follow registry/effects/scan-reveal-image, which is the reference for animated image effects, and remember that verify fails any task over 50 ms. Set meta.capture to 5000 so the review capture shows the picture fully inked; at 1200 ms it must already be a legible halftone of the whole subject at about two thirds of its final density. It is wrong if the picture appears from an edge or in blocks, and wrong if the dots clump. Declare the facets animated, image, canvas, and dither, and let meta.palette list fg. Dither components have 6144 bytes and this one is expected near 4.6 KB. It fetches nothing, adds no dependency, takes every random number from the seed, and looks finished and intentional on both grounds.

components.title: Dither Noise
components.brief: A slow field of cloud built from fractal noise and screened into two, three, or four flat tones, drifting across the host like weather on a printed map. It is a quiet background for type, and it should read as printed rather than rendered: flat areas of even tone with a visible dot texture between them, no hue, no glow, and nothing brighter than the words in front of it. It follows Perlin's improved gradient noise for the field, summed over a few octaves through lib/noise.ts, and Ulichney's Digital Halftoning for the screen, which is where the two masks come from: a dispersed blue-noise mask, which gives a photographic face, and a clustered-dot mask of the kind Holladay described, which gives a newsprint face. Both come from lib/dither-mask.ts. One seeded noise tile is built once, at a size that wraps, and scrolled; the field is never recomputed per frame, and two layers scrolling at different rates give the drift its life. The default frame at 1200 ms has 40 to 60 percent of the frame inked, two or three tone bands clearly separated, a soft diagonal drift, and no seam where the tile wraps. It is wrong if it churns: a feature should take 20 seconds or more to cross the host. Declare the facets animated, background, canvas, and dither, and let meta.palette list fg. Dither components have 6144 bytes and this one is expected near 4.8 KB. It fetches nothing, adds no dependency, takes every random number from the seed, and looks finished and intentional on both grounds.

components.title: Dither Waves
components.brief: Two or three straight wave trains crossing at different angles. Where their crests coincide the field is dark and where they cancel it is light, and that interference is screened into flat bands, which is the moire figure printers know from overlaid screens. It is a background with structure, an ordered alternative to noise, and it should read as geometric and periodic, never random. It follows Amidror's account of the moire phenomenon between periodic layers, from which it takes one working fact: the visible figure is the beat between the layers, so a change of a few degrees or a few pixels of period moves the figure a long way, and the interesting settings all sit close together. The screen is an ordered mask from lib/dither-mask.ts, per the ordered dithering entry. Each train's phase varies along one axis only, so a row table and a column table per train are enough and a frame costs a sum and a lookup per pixel. The default frame at 1200 ms shows three trains at roughly 0, 27, and 63 degrees making a clear lattice of light and dark cells, about half the frame inked, drifting slowly enough that the lattice looks still at a glance. It is wrong if it strobes: when a period approaches the pixel scale the figure crawls violently, so keep periods well above the pixel scale and the speed low. Declare the facets animated, background, canvas, and dither, and let meta.palette list fg. Dither components have 6144 bytes and this one is expected near 4.2 KB. It fetches nothing, adds no dependency, takes every random number from the seed, and looks finished and intentional on both grounds.

components.title: Dither Stipple Image
components.brief: A photograph drawn as round dots of one size, spaced further apart where the picture is light and closer where it is dark, like a hand-stippled engraving. It should read as a drawing made of points: even spacing, no rows, no grid, and a silhouette carried by density alone. It follows Secord's weighted Voronoi stippling for the target, which is a point set whose local density follows image tone and whose spacing stays even, with no crowding and no holes. It does not run his relaxation. A blue-noise mask from lib/dither-mask.ts reaches the same target directly, because such a mask is an evenly spaced point set at every threshold, and the threshold at each pixel is the tone there. Say so plainly in the code comments: the mask stands in for the relaxation, and the test is Secord's, which is that a flat mid grey shows no rows, no clumps, and no holes. Dots are filled circles of `dotSize` in the ink color, so the result is round dots rather than square pixels, and the whole picture is recomputed on resize, on a prop change, and when the image loads. The default frame shows the built-in lit sphere as an even field of dots, dense at the terminator, thinning to bare ground at the highlight, with a clean edge. It is wrong if the dots line up in rows, which means the mask is being sampled on a grid rather than per pixel, and wrong if dots grow large enough to merge into blobs in the shadows. Declare the facets static, image, canvas, and dither, and let meta.palette list fg. Dither components have 6144 bytes and this one is expected near 4.4 KB. It fetches nothing, adds no dependency, takes every random number from the seed, and looks finished and intentional on both grounds.

components.title: Dither Crosshatch Image
components.brief: A photograph drawn in pen hatching. One set of parallel strokes carries the lightest tone that takes any ink, a second set crosses it as the picture darkens, then a third and a fourth, so the deepest shadows are a dense mesh and the highlights are bare ground. It follows Praun and colleagues' real-time hatching, whose central idea is the tonal art map: the hatch layers are built so that every stroke in a lighter layer also appears in the darker ones, which keeps strokes from appearing and vanishing as tone changes. Take that nesting rule and nothing else: a layer switches on above its own tone threshold and its strokes stay for every darker tone. Strokes are one-pixel lines at the angles in `angles`, spaced by `spacing`, clipped to the pixels whose tone reaches that layer's threshold, with a small seeded jitter along each stroke so it reads as drawn rather than printed; the picture is prepared once through lib/pixels.ts and redrawn on resize. The default frame shows the built-in lit sphere with a single hatch across the mid tones, two crossing near the terminator, the highlight left bare, and the silhouette carried by where the hatching stops rather than by an outline. It is wrong if all the layers switch on at once, which turns the picture into a flat grey mesh with no drawing left in it, so spread the thresholds across the range; and wrong if the hatching runs over the ground outside the subject. Declare the facets static, image, canvas, and dither, and let meta.palette list fg. Dither components have 6144 bytes and this one is expected near 4.3 KB. It fetches nothing, adds no dependency, takes every random number from the seed, and looks finished and intentional on both grounds.

components.title: Dither Contours
components.brief: A slow noise landscape read as a map. Height is cut into even bands, each band filled with a flat dither tone that steps darker with elevation, and every boundary drawn as a hairline, which is the terraced look of a hypsometric map. It should read as a printed relief map: calm, ordered, and legible from low to high. It follows Imhof's relief presentation for the discipline, which is that the tone sequence is monotonic, the band interval is constant, and the boundary is crisp; and the hypsometric tints entry for the convention that tone is assigned by elevation band rather than by slope. Take from both that bands never cross, the hairline sits exactly on the boundary, and the darkest tone belongs to the highest band alone. Every `index` bands the boundary is drawn in the accent, which is the index contour cartographers draw heavier. The field drifts slowly, so the bands migrate like weather, and a band takes 30 seconds or more to cross the host. The default frame at 1200 ms shows five or six bands filling the frame with clear closed contours, the highest band a small island rather than half the picture, and every boundary a continuous hairline. It is wrong if the band edges jitter by a pixel from frame to frame, which reads as noise: quantize the height, not the screen. Declare the facets animated, background, canvas, and dither, and let meta.palette list fg and accent. Dither components have 6144 bytes and this one is expected near 4.6 KB. It fetches nothing, adds no dependency, takes every random number from the seed, and looks finished and intentional on both grounds.

components.title: Dither Poster Image
components.brief: A photograph reduced to a few flat tones where the steps between tones are not hard edges but narrow dithered gradients, so it reads as a screen print with clean fields and stippled transitions. It sits deliberately between two components the catalog already has: registry/effects/duotone-image posterizes with hard steps, and registry/dither/dither-image screens the whole picture. This one keeps the fields flat and screens only near a threshold. It follows Ulichney's Digital Halftoning for how an ordered mask behaves at a threshold, and the ordered dithering entry for the Bayer matrix, which is one of its two masks; the other is the blue-noise mask from lib/dither-mask.ts. Take from them that a mask applied at a step turns that step into a dot gradient whose width is set by how far from the step the mask is allowed to act, and that outside the band the tone stays exactly flat. The picture is prepared once through lib/pixels.ts and redrawn on resize. The default frame shows the built-in lit sphere in four tones, its terminator carried by a band of stipple about a tenth of the tonal range wide, with the highlight and the deepest shadow completely flat. It is wrong if the whole picture is screened, which makes it dither-image again, and wrong if the band is so wide that no flat field survives. Declare the facets static, image, canvas, and dither, and let meta.palette list fg. Dither components have 6144 bytes and this one is expected near 4.3 KB. It fetches nothing, adds no dependency, takes every random number from the seed, and looks finished and intentional on both grounds.

components.title: Edge Trace Image
components.brief: A photograph reduced to its outlines: one-pixel ink lines where the picture changes fastest, and bare ground everywhere else, like a technical pen tracing. It follows the Sobel operator for the gradient at each pixel, which lib/filter.ts supplies, and Canny's approach for what to keep, from which it takes two rules and no more. First, thin the response to the ridge of the gradient rather than leaving a fat band, so a line is one pixel wide. Second, keep a pixel when it clears the high threshold, or when it clears the low threshold and touches a pixel already kept, so faint but connected lines survive while isolated specks do not. A small mean smoothing from lib/filter.ts runs first, which keeps single-pixel noise out of the gradient. Kept pixels are drawn in fg on transparent, unsmoothed, and the picture is prepared once through lib/pixels.ts and redrawn on resize. The default frame shows the built-in lit sphere as a clean closed circle with one soft interior line at the terminator and nothing else. It is wrong if the frame is a grey mist: every kept pixel has to belong to a line a reader can follow, so if the low threshold is admitting isolated pixels the picture reads as dirt rather than as drawing. Declare the facets static, image, and canvas, and let meta.palette list fg. Effects have 6144 bytes and this one is expected near 4.4 KB. It fetches nothing, adds no dependency, takes every random number from the seed, and looks finished and intentional on both grounds.

components.title: Photocopy Image
components.brief: A photograph as a bad photocopy: pure ink and pure ground, local contrast pushed until a face survives even where the original is dark, a scatter of toner specks, and short streaks trailing away from strong edges. It follows Bradley and Roth's adaptive threshold, in which each pixel is compared with the mean of a window around it rather than with one number for the whole picture, so a shadowed area keeps its detail; take that comparison and its small negative bias, which is what stops a flat area from filling with noise. Crow's summed-area table is what makes the window mean cheap at any window size, and lib/filter.ts supplies it. The specks and the streaks come from the seed alone, so the same seed always prints the same copy, and the picture is prepared once through lib/pixels.ts and redrawn on resize. The default frame shows the built-in lit sphere as a hard two-tone copy, its terminator broken into a ragged boundary, a light dusting of specks over the ground, and two or three faint streaks trailing below it. It is wrong if it looks like a plain threshold, which is what happens when the window grows to the size of the picture, and wrong if large flat areas fill with speckle, which is what happens when the bias is zero. Declare the facets static, image, and canvas, and let meta.palette list fg. Effects have 6144 bytes and this one is expected near 4.5 KB. It fetches nothing, adds no dependency, takes every random number from the seed, and looks finished and intentional on both grounds.

components.title: Risograph Image
components.brief: A photograph printed as two passes: one in fg carrying the shadows and one in the accent carrying the midtones, each screened with its own grain and offset from the other by a pixel or two, so every edge shows the fringe a risograph leaves. It follows the process itself. The duplicator's own documentation describes a machine that prints one ink per drum in one pass per drum, and the encyclopaedia entry carries the arrangement that matters here, which is that a second colour means a second pass and the paper does not return to exactly the same place. Take the offset from that, not from a filter. Each pass is screened with a void-and-cluster blue-noise mask, per Ulichney, from lib/dither-mask.ts, rotated differently for each pass so the two grains never agree and no moire forms. The picture is prepared once through lib/pixels.ts and redrawn on resize. Only two inks appear, fg and accent, over the ground; never a third hue. The default frame shows the built-in lit sphere with the accent pass on the lit side, the fg pass in the shadow, a visible one-pixel accent fringe along the upper left of the silhouette, and grain coarse enough to see at arm's length. It is wrong if it comes out clean: without the offset and the grain it is registry/effects/duotone-image, which the catalog already has, and the roughness of the print is the whole component. Declare the facets static, image, canvas, and dither, and let meta.palette list fg and accent. Effects have 6144 bytes and this one is expected near 4.7 KB. It fetches nothing, adds no dependency, takes every random number from the seed, and looks finished and intentional on both grounds.

components.title: Channel Shift Image
components.brief: A photograph split into two flat layers, one holding the dark tones and one the light, each posterized to a single tone and then slid apart along one axis, so the picture reads doubled at every edge like a print whose passes never lined up. It follows printing registration, which is the alignment of one pass to the next; when registration fails, the passes separate along one direction by the same amount everywhere. Take that constancy: every part of a layer moves by the same offset, nothing is warped, and nothing is softened. It has to stay clearly distinct from registry/effects/risograph-image, which is grainy and offset by a pixel. This one is clean: no grain, no screen, hard tone edges, and an offset large enough to read as deliberate, where a twelfth of the picture's width is not too much. Where the two layers overlap, `overlap` decides whether the ink accumulates into a darker third area or the upper layer simply covers the lower. The picture is prepared once through lib/pixels.ts and redrawn on resize. The default frame shows the built-in lit sphere as two crescents, one fg and one accent, separated by about 8 px horizontally, with the overlap reading as a third and darker shape. It is wrong with three or more layers, and wrong when the offset is small enough to be mistaken for a rendering mistake. Declare the facets static, image, and canvas, and let meta.palette list fg and accent. Effects have 6144 bytes and this one is expected near 4.0 KB. components.title: Pixel Displace Image
components.brief: A photograph cut into horizontal bands that slide sideways by different amounts, the amounts coming from a slow noise field, so the picture shears and re-forms like a printout pulled crooked as it came out. The picture stays the picture: displacement reaches a few percent of the width at most, and the subject is never unreadable. It follows Perlin's improved gradient noise, sampled once per band per frame through lib/noise.ts, and takes from it the smooth band-limited character, which means neighbouring bands mostly move by similar amounts, so the shear reads as a wave passing through the picture rather than as hash. The amplitude rises and falls over the cycle, so the picture settles to no displacement at all for part of every pass. The picture is prepared once when the image loads and when the host resizes, on a copy no wider than 480 px, as registry/effects/pixel-sort already does; each frame draws at most 200 strips from that prepared copy and nothing reads pixels back per frame. Follow registry/effects/scan-reveal-image, which is the reference for animated image effects, and remember that verify fails any task over 50 ms. The default frame at 1200 ms sits mid-cycle, with a clear stepped shear across the middle third and the top and bottom nearly aligned. It is wrong when the strips are so thin or so many that the subject dissolves, and wrong when a frame costs a pixel read. Declare the facets animated, image, and canvas, and let meta.palette list fg. components.title: Slit Scan Image
components.brief: A photograph rebuilt column by column, where the column drawn at each position is taken from somewhere else in the picture, and where that somewhere moves with a slit travelling across the frame. Part of the subject stretches into long streaks while the rest compresses, and the whole picture breathes as the slit passes. It follows Golan Levin's catalogue of slit-scan work for the definition of the form: a one-dimensional slice of a source is recorded over time and the slices are laid side by side, so one axis of the result is space and the other is time. Take that discipline. One output column takes exactly one source slice, and the frame is never warped as a whole. Source positions are rounded to whole pixels, so nothing is interpolated and the picture stays crisp. The picture is prepared once when the image loads and when the host resizes, on a copy no wider than 480 px, as registry/effects/pixel-sort already does; each frame draws columns from that prepared copy and nothing reads pixels back per frame. Follow registry/effects/scan-reveal-image, which is the reference for animated image effects, and remember that verify fails any task over 50 ms. The default frame at 1200 ms puts the slit about a third of the way across, with the subject clearly recognisable on one side and drawn out into long streaks on the other. It is wrong when nothing of the subject survives: at every moment at least half the frame has to be readable as the picture. Declare the facets animated, image, and canvas, and let meta.palette list fg. Effects have 6144 bytes and this one is expected near 4.5 KB. It fetches nothing, adds no dependency, takes every random number from the seed, and looks finished and intentional on both grounds.
